noticias.titulo: Is this the future of America?
noticias.resumen: In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a […]
noticias.contenido: In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a “real job” and stumbled into a role at Loudoun’s economic development authority. This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the county’s revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the county’s tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst — those of the dot-com era. The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the US’s largest internet provider . Combined with its proximity to the nation’s capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planet’s internet traffic passed through Loudoun County. But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOL’s disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: “And so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,” he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. “And so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.” Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, it’s home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residents’ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools. The county’s data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the county’s operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008. Some longtime residents never heard of their county’s nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too. The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of “compute” — the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center , with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and “there’s more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.” Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, it’s the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, it’s the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, they’re beginning to wonder how much more they can take. As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this year’s midterm elections. New York and Texas have begun pumping the brakes on new data center buildouts, worried about how their energy grids could support them without leaving residents stuck holding the bag if major tech players change plans. Local stories from around the country show that residents are coming out to community meetings in droves to oppose data centers. In at least one case, a violent attack on a local Indianapolis official appeared motivated by his support for data centers. And national polls show that many Americans do not want to live near them . With its long history hosting data centers, Loudoun residents have more recently taken to calling it something new: the canary in the coal mine of data center development. Want to know what the country’s future looks like? Loudoun County’s past gives a strong glimpse of it. Even in Loudoun, where the existence of data centers has been a fact of life for nearly two decades, Rizer says that in the last few years, community opposition has become more vocal. “Before then, people understood what we were doing,” he says. These days, residents seem more aware of the inconveniences. Rizer is no stranger to this kind of response to his projects, but the tone of the pushback is different. Residents have always had myriad worries: economic, environmental, and aesthetic. That part isn’t new. “I’ve done $70 billion of deals here, and the only thing in common is that somebody’s been against every single one of them,” Rizer says. “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Asked to put his radio DJ hat on to choose a soundtrack for this moment, he chuckles and says the first one that jumps into his head is Taylor Swift’s “You Need to Calm Down.” As Rizer and other officials in Loudoun field their own residents’ concerns about data centers, they’re also being flooded with calls from local officials across the country looking for their advice. Rizer is the first to admit that hosting a data center, let alone hundreds, is not the right choice for every community. He stands by the work he’s done to bring them to Loudoun, and still believes they’ve benefited the county on the whole. But data center expansion in Loudoun has recently taken on a life of its own, to the point that even Rizer no longer spends his time courting new facilities. “We don’t want more data centers here, but we want those that are here to be successful and continue to contribute to our community,” he says, diplomatically. But new facilities are coming anyway, and even Rizer, the “ godfather of data centers ,” is powerless to stop them. Over a series of visits to Loudoun County, I wanted to see for myself what it’s like to cross through communities surrounded by the cloud. Is the data center future that so many across the country seem to fear all it’s been built up to be? “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Long before it became Data Center Alley, Loudoun County was already solidifying its role as the hometown of the modern internet. In 1996, AOL decided to move its headquarters from neighboring Fairfax County to Loudoun, eventually employing more than 5,000 workers in Ashburn at its peak in 2004. Soon, the first internet exchange point, MAE-East, would make a similar move to Ashburn , making Loudoun the physical location where much of the world’s internet traffic flowed. It was further solidified as a tech juggernaut when telecom company MCI WorldCom also opened a large office in the area, which became its headquarters in 2003 . The companies brought more than just jobs and a new workforce to the area. They also laid fiber underground across the county, attracting other tech firms to the area because of the convenient promise of low latency and proximity to the nation’s capital. The attention earned Loudoun nicknames like “ the Silicon Valley of the East ” and “ Dulles Technology Corridor ,” after the nearby airport. For a while, AOL and MCI’s presence made Loudoun an unlikely but bustling tech hub. Between 1990 and 2000, the county population doubled to 170,000 . Early AOL employees have recounted lavish parties thrown by the company in its heyday, including “go-go-style dancers” and a sushi conveyor belt around an airplane at the nearby annex of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. During this time, data centers were already starting to pop up in Loudoun County, but with little fanfare. The first one arrived in 1997, and after that there was a slow drip of new data centers permitted in the area. In 2000, the local zoning administrator made a decision that would have lasting consequences later on, but made little noise at the time. Because data centers looked similar to offices, they became designated as “office parks,” meaning that they could be built on any land zoned for office space “by right” — bypassing more time-intensive regulatory review. That meant that unlike other commercial facilities like heavy machinery plants, which face more restrictions being built near populated residential areas, data centers could be built wherever offices had been allowed. Then the dot-com bubble burst. In early 2000, AOL announced a blockbuster merger with Time Warner for more than $160 billion. But as the first wave of internet companies suffered sharp declines, AOL’s ad revenue tanked, and the country’s largest provider of dial-up internet was soon undercut further by the rise of faster cable broadband. MCI filed for bankruptcy in 2002 after a major accounting scandal. By 2006, it was acquired by Verizon , and a year later, a much diminished AOL announced it would move its headquarters to New York. Soon after came the financial downturn that became the Great Recession. Looking for unique ways to pitch the county, Rizer, then a newly minted business development manager, saw an opportunity in the recently emptied buildings and miles of fiber still lacing Loudoun’s roads. From 2002 to 2005, no new data centers had been permitted. In the years after Rizer began courting them, only a few were permitted per year, county data shows, but growth was slow and steady. Then, in 2014, the number of data centers permitted jumped to seven. Rizer recalls feeling like the county could finally start relying less on its taxes from residents and more on commercial revenue. “We were catching up on schools and catching up on salaries for our workforce,” he says. He recalls no pushback out of the ordinary on any development project, and says that for 15 years, “everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community.” In 2018, data center permits tripled to 21 in a year, and they reached a new peak in 2022 at 25. Only those who were really paying attention seemed to notice that Loudoun was quickly becoming the data center capital of the world. Many longtime residents I spoke to sheepishly admit they hardly recognized Loudoun’s global reputation for data centers, though they perhaps passively noticed the new, blocky buildings that popped up along main roads or the tall transmission towers near their favorite running trail. Over the past 20 years, though, Loudoun residents have seen a direct impact of data centers on their lives, whether they knew it or not. Real property tax rates declined dramatically, while property values have gone up in some communities as much as 182 percent in the last decade, even at residences close to data centers, according to county officials. The county has paved smooth roads and built sprawling athletic fields, a recreation center with an Olympic-size pool, and an average of nearly one and a half state-of-the-art public school buildings every year for the past 15 years, all thanks largely to the revenue generated by the county taxes data center companies have to pay anytime they get new equipment. And while data centers have gotten a reputation for creating relatively few jobs once they’re constructed, the county says that for every job inside those buildings, three and a half non-construction jobs are “supported” throughout the rest of the state economy. Those include ongoing maintenance at data centers, like electricians or HVAC technicians, and employment at other tech companies that move to Loudoun to be near where the data lives. While the data centers take advantage of a long-standing tax exemption from the state, Rizer emphasizes that the county has never spent a dime to attract them to the area. “A majority of the people that live here now only know prosperity, only know the strongest local economy in the country, only know great services and great schools,” Rizer says. “And so they don’t necessarily connect to that. They don’t see that common thread between the fact that the data centers are here and they have a great quality of life.” My most recent visit to Loudoun is on a July day when wildfire smoke that’s wafted down from Canada has sent air quality into a Code Purple . The ashy filter makes the grayish buildings all around look especially drab, though when I visit a local bike trail lined with trees and transmission towers, I still see plenty of cyclists braving the AQI that exceeds 200 in some spots. Julie Bolthouse, a longtime Loudoun resident who grew up across northern Virginia, drives me by the old AOL campus and points out a building with a playground on the other side of the street. “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here,” she says. “Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.” The lot where the old AOL campus sat is now filled with construction equipment and several-story buildings. The old headquarters has been demolished to make way for — you guessed it — more data centers. Throughout Loudoun, Bolthouse remembers land that now houses data centers being home to business centers and dentist’s offices. She returned to the area after college, enjoying that it made an easy trip to both DC and Virginia’s Shenandoah National Park, and feeling comfortable in an area that’s generally not prone to major weather events like hurricanes. In 2017, the organization she joined, Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), began tracking the impact of data centers on the local environment. A year later, Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors had one of its most contentious votes ever, narrowly approving a 750,000-square-foot data center spanning over 100 wooded acres near Goose Creek. Groups like PEC loudly objected to the development over environmental concerns, while those in favor of the proposal argued development would happen there regardless; it was just a matter of what would get built. “Everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community” Today, Bolthouse is the director of land use at PEC and helps lead a coalition of Virginia groups that advocate for stronger protections, tracking, and transparency around data center development. Bolthouse isn’t dispositionally anti-data center, nor does she want to see existing ones in the area torn down or shut off. But she does advocate for a pause on new development. “This industry is kind of creating a narrative that they’re up against communities, and that there’s a community backlash, and we just need to explain to the communities the benefits of data centers,” she says. “But what they’re really up against is physics. They’re up against the reality of what it takes to build out gigawatts of power, and the impact of building out gigawatts of power has direct impacts on people.” Recently, she’s found, more of her neighbors are paying attention. She recalls 2025 as a turning point, where PEC no longer had to do the legwork to get people invested, but instead was triaging which press requests would make the most impact given its limited capacity. And for residents, data centers were becoming more than just eyesores. They were beginning to disrupt life in Loudoun. Vicky Hu lives in a red brick home on a cul-de-sac beside a peaceful, tree-lined stream. Her backyard stretches far along the water, where a white gazebo gives shade to sit and watch the deer she says regularly cross her yard. Including her mother and daughter, three generations of Hu’s family have lived in this house. Having grown up in the city of Taipei, Hu marveled at the nature that surrounded her new home: deer as well as turtles and cranes. “To me, this is like a dream. My dream home,” she tells me. Until last year, when Hu got a call that pierced that dream. She got a voicemail from a Dominion Energy representative and first wondered if there was an issue with her energy bill payment. Instead, she was told that a new transmission line connecting two substations would cut directly through her backyard. “Are you out of your fucking mind?” she yelled at the rep. On the day I visit, the gazebo is filled with poster boards of blown-up maps of the community — and new development plans that threaten to overtake it. The trees along the stream are tagged with bright pink ribbons tied around their trunks. They mark the land Hu’s family says would be cleared should Dominion Energy’s plan to string 185-foot transmission towers through their backyard go through as planned. “It’s like the sort of thing you only think you’d see in a dystopian nightmare,” Hu’s daughter, 23-year-old Madison Taggart, tells me as she shows me around her childhood home. Growing up, Taggart says that home always felt “like a timeless place that no one else could touch.” Hu bought it shortly after her daughter was born, having seen the community built from the ground up. She worked for a developer and recalls watching workers bury power and communication lines beneath the community from her trailer across the road. By 2003, she’d nearly finished selling the community, except for one lot that was reserved for a VP at her company. As Hu’s aging mother struggled with the stairs in her townhome, she kept thinking about that lot on the cul-de-sac next to the water. She asked her colleague if she could buy it, and two years later, she moved in. Now, Hu is engaged in a yearlong fight to redirect the transmission line to another route — one that, so far, she’s on the losing end of, pending an appeal to the Supreme Court of Virginia. After that first phone call, Hu said she ran around the neighborhood “like a crazy woman,” ringing doorbells and asking if anyone had heard of the proposal. She said they hadn’t. By the time I visit, a sign in her backyard shows a diagram of the proposed 185-foot transmission tower next to a comparatively stout Statue of Liberty (if you exclude the base she stands on). “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here. Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.” Dominion insists that building the transmission line is necessary to power not only data centers, but also homes, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The local school district has been dragged into the fight over the route as well, though, with one proposal cutting close to two nearby schools. Hu’s homeowners association donated a portion of land that would be cut through to the school district, preventing it from being seized by eminent domain. Both the school district and residents in Hu’s community have been fighting the planned routes, and worry that the expansion could signal even more encroachment on key facets of the community down the road. “There’s also a deep concern for having this be a precedent that it could normalize easing the planning by just putting them on school property,” says April Chandler, Loudoun County School Board chair. Her concerns are with the kids and faculty of her community. “As a school board member, it’s not my job necessarily to consider what’s best for Dominion Energy or for data centers.” Despite working or living in Loudoun since 2000, Hu had never heard the nickname “Data Center Alley” until last year, when a Swiss reporter came to interview her about life in the data center capital of the world. Now, she can’t unhear it. She notices transmission towers everywhere she goes. And she worries nowhere is truly safe from the ever-expanding buildout. “This is just the first power line coming through a neighborhood. Where do you think the rest of the power lines [are] going to go through?” she asks. She predicts that in the next five to 10 years, “when you look at the sky in Ashburn … you’re going to see a power line running everywhere, like a spiderweb.” Should she lose the fight to preserve her backyard, Hu says she’d have no choice but to leave. “Do I want to stay here sitting on my deck watching the power pole? … Or should I stay here for a couple years to see if I’m going to get cancer or a brain tumor?” She has lost sleep and hair fretting over how to save her home this past year. “It’s just very sad,” she says. “You‘re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’” As I get out of the car a couple blocks down from the Vantage VA2 data center, I can already hear the whirring. Because I visited on a day with such poor air quality, what I’m told are usually invisible emissions plumes make a faint outline in the smoggy air. They’re emitted, Bolthouse tells me, by the diesel generators powering the facility. She compares the noise to that of a lawn mower. (I later find out that the generators are never supposed to run on day with such poor air quality, but an emergency circuit issue required them to kick in temporarily.) It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise, nearby residents like Lindsay Shaw tell me. We meet while she’s out for a walk with her dog, and she describes the way the sound permeates into her home. Constant light from the data center shines right into her bedroom at night unless the bathroom door is fully closed. Her fiancé has taken to wearing an eye mask. Nobody wanted it this way. In an ideal world, Vantage would have done what hundreds of other data centers in the area have done and connected to the Dominion energy grid by the time the site went online last year. But after Vantage had already signed agreements with customers leasing space in the new data center, Dominion informed Vantage it didn’t have enough capacity to get the 800,000-square-foot data center on the grid. Rather than let the building sit dormant until Dominion built up capacity, Vantage decided to create its own energy source using gas turbines. This is becoming more and more common in other parts of the country, as the new AI-motivated data centers require vastly more energy than the old cloud servers. Residents and local politicians acknowledge that the Vantage site is an outlier because of its unusual reliance on on-site generated power from natural gas — albeit a very annoying one. Before it was built, Shaw tells me she thought a data center would be among the best options that could come to the lot across the street, in part because it wouldn’t be something that would drive a lot of traffic near what she says is an already dangerous intersection. But now she says the data center has caused plenty of other problems and feels the operators have not been proactive enough in engaging neighbors. Vantage’s senior vice president of global public policy, John Stephenson, says he “would respectfully disagree” that they haven’t proactively engaged nearby residents. He notes that they held a community meeting at a nearby brewery to field questions early on, but admits that “in retrospect, we probably could have done more.” The company has taken different approaches to mitigate the noise, including installing insulation and repositioning the turbines to lower their tone. But residents who live near other data centers throughout Loudoun — even those that don’t have to generate their own power on-site — also complain of noise. Jason Mello says he hears a constant “low-frequency drone” he attributes to the HVAC systems of nearby data centers from his Ashburn home. Living near Dulles Airport, many Ashburn residents are used to the sound of planes overhead, “but planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.” Mello shows me videos of the noise from his deck outside a town hall meeting where we meet. He says he’s already spent $2,600 getting two new window inserts, with three more to go in his bedroom. He was quoted at least $15,000 for new siding that would further mitigate the noise. “As a homeowner, if I want to live in peace at night, that addresses the inside,” he says, “but if I’m sitting on my deck, I can constantly hear that humming. And I think that’s why you got to fix the problem also at the source.” “You’re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’” Several residents tell me that the boom in infrastructure needed to support the data centers has impacted their ability to enjoy the natural resources of Loudoun that once attracted them. “You can barely hear the birds anymore,” says Jessica Medeiros, another resident who lives across the street from the Vantage data center. Even when she tries to retreat from the noise near her home, she’s regularly reminded of the data centers’ presence. As a regular runner on the famed Washington and Old Dominion trail for the past 20 years, Medeiros says the “constant construction,” towering power lines, and reduced shade because of cleared trees “ruins the experience with nature.” She often says that when she dies, “I want my ashes scattered along the trail. But I think that trail’s going to look a lot different in another 10 years.” “The greenery is gone. The sense of community is gone. It feels very stale,” says Jenny Marza, another Loudoun County resident. “There’s no more trees left and every inch is taken up by greed.” While fighting new development near her own home, Marza has already felt pressure from the data center explosion on her small export logistics business. For years she’s been looking at buying office and warehouse space in the area to be near the airport, but prices have been so astronomical that she’s been forced to continue leasing. Now, even her current office rent has skyrocketed — she suspects because every landlord knows that data centers are willing to pay an average of $3.76 million per acre . It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise. Marza says “I’m kicking myself” over a warehouse she came close to buying last year for around $5 million, but held off because it was more space than she needed at the time. “And then we put a pause on the search for two years and when we returned, it was like, ‘Holy crap, there’s nothing left.’” Anything that was selling at $5 million was now $10 million. To Marza, the residential property tax savings and increased home values mean little when compared to the quality-of-life concerns she has and the ability to help her small business survive. “I feel like it’s a drop in the ocean of what they’re getting in return,” she says. “I feel like nobody protected our interests as a community.” “Done the right way, you can be good neighbors,” Shaw says, reflecting on the Vantage site near her home. “But this one was done like that shady neighbor next door that has people coming in and out all hours of the night. And then the FBI raids them and you’re like, ‘Well, I knew something shady was going on.’” When I arrive at the Loudoun government building on a July evening shortly before 6:30PM, I’m handed a red flyer outside by a group advocating for local government control of utilities used to power data centers. Inside, the nearly full room is prominently speckled with light blue shirts that read “I support data centers.” The shirts list the reasons: “Because I like: lower taxes, excellent schools, better job opportunities.” They also include caveats: “When they are: in the right location, well-designed, quiet, environmentally sensitive.” The slogan doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue. I comfortably score a seat, but later hear complaints from some attendees who say they arrived shortly after me and were relegated to the overflow room. Though it’s a first-come-first-served event, those critical of data centers grumble that industry supporters seem suspiciously well organized in their early arrivals. Still, it doesn’t have the kind of fireworks or soundbites that have made community meetings about data centers around the country into national news. While some residents voice strong frustration, the two-and-a-half-hour forum is cordial and respectful of Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall’s request of no cheering nor jeering. “Planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.” Randall is in a tough spot. As head of the elected nine-member panel tasked with adopting local ordinances, appropriating funds, and rezoning land, Randall has just enough power for her constituents to lay responsibility for their criticism at her feet, yet not enough to change some of the things she says she wishes she could. At the meeting, she listens to residents’ concerns, promising to follow up with phone calls for some while repeatedly acknowledging and lamenting the quality-of-life frustrations many of her neighbors have about living near data centers. But she also declines to give ground on topics she said are unfounded or detached from political reality. Randall walks residents through the history of data centers in Loudoun, including what they are and how they came to be zoned the same way as office parks. Before getting to the audience participation portion, she clicks to a slide that says “4 Things That Are Unpopular But True” with a grimace emoji. The first: At one point in time, residents actually preferred data centers over new housing developments. She references opposition to a 2021 proposal to build up to 779 residential housing units in Ashburn, called Hyde Park. Across about 125 comments, residents reportedly worried about increased traffic and infrastructure strain. Nearly two years after submitting the application, the developer withdrew and decided to establish a by-right data center there instead. “One of my worst days was January 5th, 2023, when the applicant called me and said, ‘Forget it. I’m going to go build a data center,’” Randall says. “And I pretty much begged them not to.” “So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?” The second unpopular truth: It’s not legal for Loudoun to enact a moratorium on development without the state’s permission. Third: Both the Biden and Trump administrations have indicated AI infrastructure buildout will be a national priority, so that’s unlikely to change anytime soon. And fourth: Despite resident backlash to certain data center land use exceptions the board has granted, the alternative would have been that those data centers could take the land by right anyway, with much less in return. The lesson being, if data centers can break ground whether government officials want them to or not, the county might as well get something out of it. Residents who speak at the hearing do not dispute her account of the county’s history. Many express frustration about the buildings encroaching on greenery or creating annoying and near-constant noise issues. But many others, including several in the blue shirts, argue in support of data centers as stewards of the community they are proud to be known for. One Ashburn resident describes a peaceful experience living across from a data center. “When the weather is good, I’ll open my bedroom windows, from which I can see it directly. It is silent, it is clean. It is a good neighbor,” he says. Another resident, who leads the nonprofit Northern Virginia Science Center Foundation, credits data centers with generating revenue that can help fund such endeavors to a greater degree than it sees in nearby Fairfax. The organization lists Loudoun County, Dominion Energy, and data center company QTS among its partners. Randall affirms residents’ data center complaints, but also fact-checks several claims about supposed data center projects she says never existed in the first place. One Ashburn resident, for example, bemoans what he calls the “Ashburn Commons proposal” that would create a blight next to existing housing, greenery, and other community institutions. Randall asks him to clarify if he is thinking about a proposal near the Harris Teeter grocery store. “Yes!” he answers. “That’s not real,” Randall says. Her colleague adds the would-be developer hasn’t even submitted a formal application for it, and the government had denied an initial request. “Well,” the resident cries out, “praise the Lord on that!” “I don’t want to be the example of what not to do.” For all the gripes, I’ve still yet to meet anyone in Loudoun County who actually says they oppose data centers entirely. Whether they’re currently living next to gas turbines or their backyard could potentially be seized to build a transmission tower, Loudoun residents still recognize that data centers help power the technology we use every day. After all, they need to go somewhere . Why not there? But even if Loudoun residents have accepted the economic benefits as a tradeoff for the loud eyesores near their homes, it doesn’t mean they’re open to an expansion of that deal. “It’s not about trying to get rid of the existing data centers. These data centers are here. They’re running. I don’t want them to go anywhere,” Bolthouse says. “The question isn’t, ‘Do we need data centers?’ The question is, ‘Is it worth threatening our air quality, threatening our water supply, and throwing our communities into chaos, and taking people’s private land for transmission lines to get it?’” I spoke with over half a dozen Loudoun residents, and universally, this is what they want communities considering data centers to understand: Know what you’re getting into. That means making sure existing laws and ordinances will apply to data centers, that local utilities have a plan to ensure enough capacity for the expected buildout, and that neither data centers nor the infrastructure needed to power them can be built too close to homes or schools. Even Rizer says the buildout in Loudoun has, in some places, gone beyond what he’d have hoped. “There’s no data centers here that aren’t where they’re allowed to be, but I think sometimes there’s a difference between what you’re allowed to do and what is probably best for the community,” he says. “And that’s what we’ve had to clean up a little bit.” At the town hall, Randall showed aerial images of several residential communities that were directly bordered by data centers. Those arrangements are not what any Loudoun official or resident considers ideal — but even so, she said, property values in those communities have only gone up. There are limits. Loudoun hasn’t had a strategic focus on bringing in more data centers since 2019, Rizer says. More recently, the local government is pursuing a plan to pump the brakes further — doing away with the ability for data centers to use office-zoned land by right, and considering pausing new permit reviews while contemplating zoning changes that could better address community impacts. When peers around the country contact him about whether they should invite data centers into their communities, Rizer says, “It’s not right for every place. So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?” For Loudoun, unlike many yet-to-be-developed areas in the US, there is a definitive end in sight. The county has an ever-diminishing amount of space left to develop data centers, after which point it will continue to collect tax revenue when the companies update equipment within their walls. Loudoun residents hope that by the time it gets to that point, the things that they love about the area are still there. For many, it’s the convenience of living near DC, but still close to nature. It’s also often about the quality public schools, funded in part with the revenue raised by the colossal energy-guzzling slabs in their backyards. AOL’s roots helped make Loudoun the first major data center capital, and that came with both advantages and challenges. For communities starting to consider their first data center today, Bolthouse says they’re in a much better position than Loudoun was because the industry isn’t yet “embedded” in layers of government. She still thinks their story could become a beacon of hope for others, rather than a warning — but it’s an uphill battle to get there. “I don’t want to be the example of what not to do,” she says. “I want to be the example of what to do. I want to bring journalists out to see how we fixed problems, how we are doing much better, and how communities are happy with these facilities because they’ve done something better.” Hearing Bolthouse’s frustration with the ever-expanding energy demands imposed by data centers, it’s surprising to hear her embrace the ones that are already here. But for all the friction they’ve caused in her community recently, it’s also clear from my visits and conversations that data centers have played a central role in supporting many positive aspects of life in Loudoun. The question, now, is whether Loudoun can manage its existing demand and successfully serve community needs as the data center footprint continues to grow. If Bolthouse sounds optimistic, she is certain that something has to give. In the past, Loudoun’s data center buildout was quiet and steady. Today’s is anything but. “I don’t see how that happens with the scale and speed to market that the industry is pursuing.”

noticias.titulo: Nearly 2,000-year-old vessel with two snake heads found at Roman villa in Spain
noticias.resumen: A Roman villa in Spain yielded fragments of a unique two-headed serpent vessel. This artifact suggests the private worship of the god Sabazios spread widely. Laboratory tests indicate the vessel likely originated from Roman Africa. Evidence for this cult on the Iberian Peninsula is generally scarce. The find highlights the quiet reach of ancient religious practices into rural areas.

noticias.titulo: Las tecnológicas chinas se enfrentan al Pentágono en su propia casa
noticias.resumen: Varias grandes compañías de tecnología, automoción y biotecnología de China han decidido responder a la presión de EEUU . Desde entonces muchas otras empresas chinas, como…
noticias.contenido: Varias grandes compañías de tecnología, automoción y biotecnología de China han decidido responder a la presión de EEUU . En 2024 Hesai Technology, que se dedica a la fabricación de sensores LiDAR, y DJI, que produce drones, llevaron al Pentágono ante los tribunales estadounidenses . El Departamento de Defensa de EEUU las había incluido en la lista negra de empresas vinculadas al ejército chino, y estas dos compañías estaban decididas a demostrar que esa acusación no estaba fundada para proteger su reputación y sus intereses comerciales. Desde entonces muchas otras empresas chinas, como Baidu, BYD, NIO o Tencent, entre otras, han amenazado al Pentágono con proceder de la misma manera, aunque presumiblemente todavía no han presentado una demanda. No obstante, algunas sí lo han hecho. Y es que durante los últimos tres meses Alibaba, WuXi AppTec (se dedica a la biotecnología) y CXMT han presentado una demanda formal ante un tribunal de EEUU. Esta última lo ha hecho hace tan solo cinco días. Con toda probabilidad esta nueva oleada de litigios que se está produciendo en 2026 aún no ha concluido. Y es que el éxito que por el momento está consiguiendo WuXi podría animar a otras compañías chinas a apostar por su misma estrategia. El pasado 7 de agosto el juez federal James Boasberg concedió a esta empresa una medida cautelar que impide provisionalmente al Departamento de Defensa aplicar su bloqueo mientras perdure el litigio. CXMT está decidida a defender sus intereses CXMT ( ChangXin Memory Technologies ), el mayor fabricante chino de chips de memoria DRAM, tramitó su demanda al Departamento de Defensa de EEUU el pasado 28 de agosto. Esta compañía reclama que su inclusión en la lista negra del Pentágono no está justificada debido a que sus chips de memoria cumplen los estándares JEDEC que, a grandes rasgos, definen qué requisitos tienen que satisfacer las memorias. Además, asegura que la acusación del Departamento de Defensa se sostiene sobre el anuncio de un distribuidor no autorizado que describió sus productos erróneamente como "de grado militar". En Xataka Apple acusa, OpenAI responde: así es el culebrón judicial que amenaza la salida a bolsa de Altman CXMT es una compañía esencial en el intento del Gobierno chino de alcanzar la independencia tecnológica CXMT es una compañía esencial en el intento del Gobierno chino de alcanzar la independencia tecnológica . De ella depende en gran medida que China consiga minimizar su dependencia de las memorias que fabrican las empresas surcoreanas SK hynix y Samsung, y la estadounidense Micron. CXMT sostiene que desde que el Pentágono la incluyó en su lista negra en enero de 2025 su reputación y su capacidad comercial en EEUU se han visto seriamente dañadas. Mark Shi, un abogado especializado en cumplimiento normativo que trabaja en el bufete Co-Effort Law Firm de Shanghái (China), defiende que las resoluciones judiciales que han obtenido otras compañías de tecnología chinas, como Hesai, DJI o WuXi, demuestran que los jueces estadounidenses están dispuestos a analizar minuciosamente la inclusión de las empresas chinas en la lista negra del Pentágono. Y, en consecuencia, a tomar medidas cautelares provisionales que favorecen a las compañías demandantes si procede. El conflicto que están librando CXMT y el Departamento de Defensa de EEUU pondrá a prueba, según Shi , si la vinculación de una compañía con el Ministerio de Industria de China justifica su inclusión en la lista negra . Si finalmente CXMT saliese airosa y el Pentágono tuviese que deshacer su designación sentaría un precedente que con toda probabilidad beneficiaría a otras empresas chinas en el futuro. No obstante, el resultado de este litigio ahora mismo está abierto y probablemente a la institución judicial estadounidense no va a resultarle fácil mantenerse al margen de los grupos de presión que exigen mano dura con China. noticias.contenido: Las hemos visto excluyentes. Las hemos visto que obligan a estacionar algunos coches en aparcamientos subterráneos. Las hemos visto con controles horarios. Las hemos visto fuera del centro de las ciudades. Y las hemos visto, incluso, que no sirven para nada. Pero lo que es seguro es que no habíamos visto ninguna zona de bajas emisiones (ZBE) como la de Santa Cruz de Tenerife. Las ZBE . Desde 2023, todas las ciudades con más de 50.000 habitantes tienen que tener una ZBE que mejore la calidad del aire. Eso, sin embargo, no quiere decir nada . Porque aunque la obligación está sobre la mesa, el Gobierno no diseñó ningún régimen sancionador para castigar a quienes hicieran oídos sordos. Eso ha llevado a la situación que tenemos ahora. Sí, hay ciudades repartidas por toda España que tienen su propia ZBE pero hay otras que han pasado del tema , asumiendo que implantar restricciones a sus vecinos puede tener un impacto directo en los votos que recibirán en las próximas elecciones. En Xataka Nos encantaría saber qué coches no podrán entrar por defecto en las ZBE de 2023, pero es imposible Mejor ser creativo . Pero además de que no había régimen sancionador, el Gobierno tampoco definió cómo debía ser la ZBE, apuntando a que cada ciudad tiene sus propias particularidades. Eso, ha abierto un abanico de posibilidades enorme. La ZBE de Sevilla se encuentra en un parque en lugar de el centro de la ciudad al que se puede seguir accediendo sin restricciones. La ZBE de Bilbao es extraordinariamente pequeña. La ZBE de Barcelona (que ya estaba activa antes de 2023) tiene su propio horario. La ZBE de Madrid tiene "zonas de especial protección" dentro de ella que cuentan con sus propias normas. La ZBE de Ciudad Real es, sencillamente, inexistente pese a que está activa Y es que, como decíamos, el único objetivo que el Gobierno señalaba es que se mejorara la calidad del aire. Pero tampoco quedaba claro cómo debía medirse esto ni qué sucedía si se incumplía este precepto pese a aplicar nuevas normas. Así, una ciudad puede levantar, por ejemplo, una ZBE en un polígono industrial y dejar entrar hasta el mismo casco histórico de la ciudad a cualquier coche. En Xataka "No es zona para ricos": Ciudad Real creará la única ZBE de España donde los coches sin etiqueta de la DGT son bienvenidos Y llega Santa Cruz de Tenerife . Más de tres años después de que sea obligatorio contar con una ZBE, Santa Cruz de Tenerife tiene la suya ya definida. Lo hace en una zona concreta de la ciudad que abarca "casi la totalidad de los barrios de El Toscal y Zona Centro", según leemos en la página web del Ayuntamiento . Especifican que la medida es una necesidad porque viven más de 16.000 personas en el interior de este espacio pero allí se registran más de 200.000 trayectos diarios en lo que, aseguran, es una de las zonas más concurridas de toda la isla. Para ello, además de delimitar la zona que puedes ver en este mapa , se prohíbe el acceso a los coches sin etiquetado ambiental cuyos dueños no residan en el interior de este espacio. También hay excepciones (que puedes leer en este documento) para los trabajadores habituales, los transportistas y las personas que tienen que llevar al interior de este espacio a una persona de edad avanzada o con problemas de movilidad, entre otras. En Xataka Mario Arnaldo, presidente AEA: "Madrid está actuando como una administración tramposa que solo quiere sacar los cuartos a los madrileños" Sin ITV, media vuelta . Hasta aquí, todo normal. Pero entre los requisitos para poder pasar al interior de este espacio, también se señala uno pionero en España: tener la ITV y el seguro en vigor. Y es que, aprovechando las cámaras de entrada y salida de la ZBE, la ciudad puede castigarte si accedes a la misma con la ITV o el seguro caducado. Explican en AECA-ITV, quienes llevan tiempo pidiendo que se tenga en cuenta esta medida, que la ciudad se convierte en la primera de España en imponer este requisito. Y es que, destacan con razón, que un coche con etiquetado ambiental que no haya cumplido las exigencias de la ITV en materia de emisiones puede ser mucho más contaminante que otro sin dicha pegatina pero con el examen de la ITV en regla. La nueva medida no impide el acceso a los coches con la ITV caducada si su destino es una estación ITV en el interior pero podrá sancionar por carecer de esta obligación a coches que sí tendrían permitido el acceso. La multa por no haber pasado la ITV es de 200 euros, igual que la de acceder sin autorización a una ZBE. Es decir, en ese caso un acceso incorrecto se saldaría con 400 euros de multa al conductor (200 euros de acceso a la ZBE y 200 euros por no llevar la ITV en regla). En el caso de carecer de seguro, la sanción puede alcanzar los 600 euros. En Xataka Las ZBE tienen una nueva arma en el horizonte: el primer dispositivo que detecta emisiones de los coches en tiempo real Sí, pero... Todo esto es la teoría porque, en la práctica... no hay fecha definida para la implantación de la nueva ZBE. Y es que en la web del Ayuntamiento de Santa Cruz de Tenerife sólo se especifica que el periodo de gracia antes de multar será "lo suficientemente largo para que todos entendamos el sistema y nos acostumbremos a su uso". Si acudimos a la nueva ordenanza de movilidad, entonces comprobamos que las multas no van a llegar mañana... ni a corto plazo. Y es que aquí puedes leer que las multas "serán de aplicación a los 36 meses desde la entrada en vigor de la presente Ordenanza", aunque los avisos empezarán a llegar a los conductores en año y medio. Es decir, Santa Cruza de Tenerife es la primera ciudad que recoge una sanción a los conductores que entren a su ZBE con la ITV y/o el seguro caducado. También es la que contempla, por esto mismo, las sanciones de mayor cuantía. Pero al menos no veremos estas hasta dentro de tres años. Es decir, llegará al menos seis años después de que sea obligatoria. Foto | Mike Peel y Francisco de Frias En Xataka | Se suponía que a partir del 1 de enero de 2026 los coches sin etiqueta ya no podrían circular por Madrid. noticias.contenido: Uno se pasa por el anuncio oficial de Atlas y la cosa no parece para tanto. Hace ya tiempo que los modelos de IA generativa de vídeo son capaces de crear todo tipo de escenas con un realismo fantástico. Sin embargo este nuevo modelo quiere ir más allá de la IA generativa para dar el salto a los prometedores "modelos del mundo". Atlas es el resultado de ese esfuerzo, y lo cierto es que la propuesta es llamativa por dos cosas: la primera, por cómo logra reconstruir nuestro mundo a partir de información limitada. La segunda, porque quien está detrás es Fei-Fei Li , considerada como la "madrina de la IA". Atlas no es otro generador de vídeos más . World Labs lo describe como un modelo multimodal entrenado desde cero para operar con texto, imágenes, posiciones de cámara, mapas de profundidad y secuencias de vídeo. Todos esos tipos de entrada se combinan para crear un contexto espacial común que luego permite generar nuevas observaciones que son coherentes con el espacio 3D que percibe el modelo. Técnicamente se denomina un multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer , pero aquí lo que se predice no es el siguiente token de una palabra o frase, sino lo que debería verse a continuación desde una determinada posición del espacio. Los 'modelos de mundo' apuntan a ser la próxima gran revolución de la IA: es lo que necesita la robótica para parecerse a las películas Ya has grabado, ahora mueve la cámara . En varias de las demostraciones de ese anuncio oficial se ve cómo por ejemplo hay escenas grabadas con dos o tres smartphones a partir de las cuales Atlas puede generar perspectivas que no se grabaron con niguna cámara. Las crea de la nada pero siempre manteniendo coherencia con los datos reales que sí tiene (de imágenes, grabaciones, o los citados mapas de profundidad, por ejemplo). En una entrevista con a16z , Fei-Fei Li lo expresaba claramente: "No hay lenguaje ahí fuera. No sales a la naturaleza y ves palabras escritas en el cielo para ti". Cineastas del mundo, atentos . Uno puede crear un prompt que describa una trayectoria de cámara específica y muy detallada, por ejemplo y eso permite que el modelo del mundo genere una visualización realmente convincente de esas perspectivas aun cuando nunca se grabaron con cámaras reales. Esto abre posibilidades espectaculares , como por ejemplo grabar una escena y que luego puedas colocar la cámara en sitios donde nunca estuvo para ver y mostrar a escena desde ahí. Pero Atlas no ve lo que no ocurre . Si le damos a este modelo tres fotografías de una habitación, no puede saber exactamente qué había detrás del sofá o en una esquina que ninguna cámara captó. Lo que se hace ahí es generar una solución plausible inventando contenido que sea coherente. World Labs lo resume con una frase: cuantas más imágenes recibe, menos tiene que imaginar. Más allá del cine . Aunque las aplicaciones para creadores de contenido o para la industria audiovisual y del cine son evidentes, esto puede aplicarse a campos diversos. Uno de los más prometedores es el de la robótica : Atlas puede convertir unas pocas imágenes de un lugar real en un entorno que un robot virtual puede recorrer. El modelo genera las imágenes y datos de profundidad que los sensores del robots captarían desde distintas trayectorias. La empresa lo llama real-to-sim : capturar un espacio real, convertirlo en una simulación utilizarla luego para entrenar o evaluar robots antes de dejarlos sueltos en el mundo físico real. Entrenar robots no es como entrenar a un LLM . Para enseñarle a un robot a recoger una taza necesitamos la taza, una mesa, cámaras, sensores, un robot y multitud de intentos físicos. Además ese entorno cambia: la iluminación varía, los objetos pueden moverse y las cosas pueden romperse. World Labs señala que esa es una de las grandes dificultades a la hora de sacar los robots del laboratorio. Estas simulaciones permiten repetir purebas y cometer fallos sin pagar el coste que esos fallos tendrían en el mundo real. Runway persigue algo parecido con GWM-1, por ejemplo. Bienvenidos a la "internet de los robots" . Con Atlas lo que se plantea es crear una especie de internet perfecta para el entrenamiento de robots . En lugar de estar compuesta de páginas web, estaría compuesta de cantidades enormes de espacios tridimensionales con los que poder experimentar. Atlas aún no ofrece algo así como producto completo, pero la estrategia de World Labs es la de crear modelos capaces de percibir, generar, razonar e interactuar con mundos virtuales y físicos. Los videojuegos ya dieron un paso llamativo en este ámbito . Cada juego tridimensional contiene datos como la geometría del mundo virtual, cámaras, objetos, texturas, físicas y millones de posiciones desde las que observar un escenario. Por eso emiezan a surgir empreas que quieren convertir esos mundos virtuales en formmmas de entrenar estos modelos del mundo. Los LLM se han apropiado de millones de textos y libros escritos por humanos, pero los modelos espaciales pueden aprovecharse de esos mundos virtuales que se construyeron en el mundo de los videojuegos, pero también en otros ámbitos como los simuladores o el segmento de la arquitectura. En Xataka Apple ha hecho una apuesta que en realidad es un salto al vacío: la única gran tecnológica que no está aumentando el capex De generar mundos a interactuar dentro de ellos . World Labs lleva tiempo insistiendo en una idea simple: ver no basta. La inteligencia espacial necesita entender dónde están las cosas, cómo se relacionan y qué pasa cuando actuamos sobre ellas. Atlas es de momento una primera aproximación al problema —solo está disponible con acceso anticipado para socios seleccionados— pero plantea algo distinto a los modelos de IA que nos han acompañado estos últimos años. ChatGPT y sus rivales se preguntaban qué palabra venía después, pero en Atlas la pregunta es diferente: si me muevo por aquí, qué debería ver? En Xataka | Mientras Silicon Valley se ocupaba de los agentes y el código, China se ha hecho con un área crucial de la IA: el vídeo - La noticia "No hay lenguaje ahí fuera”: Atlas quiere hacer con el mundo físico lo que los LLM hicieron con internet fue publicada originalmente en Xataka por Javier Pastor .

noticias.contenido: El análisis de restos del 3M22 Zircon está permitiendo a Ucrania mirar bajo el capó de una de las armas más secretas y propagandísticas de Rusia. Lo más inquietante de la historia es que desmontar el mito del misil de crucero hipersónico "invencible" no hace necesariamente que la amenaza sea menor: las evidencias apuntan hacia un arma posiblemente más convencional en su concepto, pero especialmente más peligrosa para unas defensas ucranianas cada vez más escasas de interceptores. Unboxing del misil “invencible”. La inteligencia militar ucraniana (GUR) ha publicado uno de los análisis más detallados hasta ahora del 3M22 Zircon, incluyendo un modelo tridimensional y un desglose de su buscador de radar, ordenador de a bordo, sistema de guiado, propulsión y cabeza de guerra. Los primeros restos identificados aparecieron tras un ataque ruso en febrero de 2024 y desde entonces Moscú ha empleado el arma en más ocasiones contra Ucrania, incluidos lanzamientos aparentemente realizados desde tierra mediante sistemas derivados del K-300P Bastion . La investigación permite por primera vez reconstruir con bastante detalle una de las armas que Rusia lleva años presentando como parte de su nueva generación de sistemas hipersónicos prácticamente imposibles de detener. En Xataka El problema ya no es que Rusia esté fabricando drones mucho más grandes y numerosos: es dónde los está haciendo La gran sorpresa. Moscú describe el Zircon como un misil de crucero hipersónico capaz de mantener velocidades extremas mediante un sistema de propulsión que respira aire, pero los restos recuperados están poniendo esa descripción en cuestión. Ucrania identifica un motor cohete de combustible sólido 3L2211 y las evidencias físicas apuntan hacia una arquitectura de dos etapas , ambas propulsadas mediante combustible sólido; además, los análisis de fuentes abiertas llevan tiempo señalando la aparente ausencia de una toma de aire convencional, un componente esencial para un ramjet o scramjet. Nada de esto demuestra al 100% que Rusia haya mentido sobre su funcionamiento, pero como apuntan los analistas , lo parece y mucho. No solo eso, refuerza una interpretación muy diferente: el Zircon apunta a ser fundamentalmente un misil cuasibalístico maniobrable y no un verdadero misil de crucero hipersónico. Lanzamiento de un Zirkon Match 9 complicado. Rusia ha asegurado que el Zircon puede alcanzar aproximadamente Mach 9 y durante una prueba de 2020 afirmó haber superado Mach 8, aunque los datos ucranianos dibujan un perfil mucho menos uniforme. El GUR recoge velocidades máximas de Mach 8-9 , pero también una velocidad máxima registrada o sostenida de Mach 6,8 , mientras otras evaluaciones ucranianas describen fases alrededor de Mach 5,5 , aceleraciones posteriores hasta aproximadamente Mach 7,5 y una nueva pérdida de velocidad antes del impacto. Eso no significa que el Zircon deje de ser hipersónico (en realidad, cualquier velocidad superior a Mach 5 entraría en esa categoría), sino que puede alcanzar esas velocidades mediante aceleración cohete y una trayectoria balística o cuasibalística, en lugar de mantener un vuelo de crucero hipersónico propulsado como sugería la imagen difundida durante años por Moscú. Menos futurística no la hace menos peligrosa. Si el análisis está en lo cierto, el Zircon podría ascender rápidamente mediante sus motores cohete, alcanzar gran altura y después dirigirse hacia el objetivo siguiendo una trayectoria parcialmente balística mientras realiza maniobras aerodinámicas y cambios de velocidad. Ese comportamiento lo convierte en más peligroso para Kiev porque puede hacerlo extraordinariamente difícil de predecir e interceptar , de una forma comparable en algunos aspectos al Kinzhal ruso: no necesita ser el sofisticado misil de crucero hipersónico que Moscú anunciaba para plantear un problema enorme a las defensas aéreas. De hecho, Ucrania asegura haber interceptado Zircon con Patriot PAC-3, demostrando que no es "invencible", pero su combinación de velocidad, altura y maniobrabilidad sigue reduciendo drásticamente el margen disponible para detectarlo, seguirlo y destruirlo. Un microchip programable en campo (FPGA) Altera Cyclone II, que según el GUR fue encontrado entre los restos del Zircon El punto débil de Kiev. La aparición del Zircon encaja además en un cambio más amplio de la campaña aérea rusa: después de que Ucrania mejorara notablemente su capacidad para destruir drones de hélice y misiles de crucero, Moscú está aumentando el peso de los misiles balísticos y de los drones a reacción, amenazas considerablemente más difíciles de detener. Según Yehor Cherniev , vicepresidente del comité parlamentario ucraniano de Seguridad Nacional, Defensa e Inteligencia, Rusia habría reducido la producción del Kinzhal debido a problemas de precisión para concentrarse en Zircon e Iskander, incluida una nueva variante Iskander-1000 . El objetivo práctico importa más que la etiqueta tecnológica: saturar a Ucrania precisamente con las armas contra las que dispone de menos soluciones eficaces. El verdadero problema. Para enfrentarse a las amenazas balísticas más complejas, Kiev depende especialmente de los Patriot estadounidenses y de sus interceptores PAC-3, cuyas existencias Ucrania lleva tiempo advirtiendo que son insuficientes. Esa es la ironía detrás del desmontaje del Zircon: Ucrania puede haber demostrado que el arma maravillosa de Putin no es exactamente lo que Rusia decía y que incluso puede ser derribada, pero al mismo tiempo Moscú está produciendo y utilizando más sistemas pertenecientes precisamente a la categoría que más recursos exige a las defensas ucranianas. Dicho de otra forma, el problema ya no consiste tanto en encontrar una respuesta técnica al supuesto misil imposible como en disponer de suficientes interceptores caros y especializados para responder a una campaña rusa cada vez más orientada hacia ese punto débil. En Xataka Los drones ucranianos se están encontrando algo extraño en el frente: "regimientos de lisiados" que supuestamente le envía Rusia La red de 70 empresas. Por último, el GUR ha identificado 70 empresas y 84 personas relacionadas con el desarrollo y fabricación del misil, encabezadas por NPO Mashinostroyeniya y acompañadas por compañías responsables del motor, buscador de radar, ordenador, guiado, cabeza explosiva y sistemas eléctricos. Entre los restos aparecen además componentes electrónicos vinculados a fabricantes estadounidenses , incluidos un amplificador asociado a TriQuint Semiconductor (actualmente parte de Qorvo) y un FPGA de Altera, hoy integrada en Intel , aunque, por supuesto, su presencia no implica que esas compañías suministraran conscientemente material a Rusia y se desconoce cómo llegó hasta su industria militar. Para Ucrania, por tanto, capturar y desmontar el Zircon ofrece una segunda oportunidad además de comprender cómo destruirlo : identificar los eslabones industriales, tecnológicos y extranjeros de una cadena de suministro rusa que puede convertirse ahora en objetivo de nuevas sanciones y controles de exportación. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness in Darkest Dungeon . Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that is Dwarf Fortress – or read about it from the mid-00s forums where…
noticias.contenido: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Bit Reactor Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM Even if you’re unfamiliar with the term “emergent storytelling”, you’ve likely experienced some of the unscripted tales that can bubble up out of a game’s systems. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness in Darkest Dungeon . Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that is Dwarf Fortress – or read about it from the mid-00s forums where users helped popularise the term “Let’s Play” by chronicling their games in descriptive posts. Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’ XCOM , the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in. Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices. As creative director Greg Foertsch puts it , “Star Wars is about loss.” Which losses you end up mourning in Zero Company depends on you. Continue reading...

noticias.titulo: Eight-letter DNA alphabet is accurately transcribed by a natural enzyme

Now, researchers at the University of California San Diego have demonstrated that one of biology's most essential enzymes can accurately read and transcribe an expanded, eight-letter genetic alphabet. The findings provide important evidence that cells can process synthetic genetic information using their natural molecular machinery, advancing a long-standing goal in synthetic biology to expand the language of DNA. It could also allow scientists to custom-engineer biological systems that perform functions or…
noticias.contenido: All known life on Earth uses the same genetic alphabet, consisting of four letters. Now, researchers at the University of California San Diego have demonstrated that one of biology's most essential enzymes can accurately read and transcribe an expanded, eight-letter genetic alphabet. The findings provide important evidence that cells can process synthetic genetic information using their natural molecular machinery, advancing a long-standing goal in synthetic biology to expand the language of DNA. It could also allow scientists to custom-engineer biological systems that perform functions or produce compounds not found in nature.

noticias.resumen: A 2002 study examined 12 artificial reefs built off Miami Beach using limestone boulders, concrete-gravel aggregate and concrete mixed with waste tyre chips. Divers surveyed the reefs every two months from October 1998 to February 2001, recording fish species, numbers and sizes, along with spiny lobsters. They counted 97,826 fish from 146 species. The researchers found no significant difference in fish abundance, biomass or species richness between the three reef materials. However, comparisons before and after deployment showed that the artificial reefs increased local fish abundance and…
noticias.contenido: A 2002 study examined 12 artificial reefs built off Miami Beach using limestone boulders, concrete-gravel aggregate and concrete mixed with waste tyre chips. Divers surveyed the reefs every two months from October 1998 to February 2001, recording fish species, numbers and sizes, along with spiny lobsters. They counted 97,826 fish from 146 species. The researchers found no significant difference in fish abundance, biomass or species richness between the three reef materials. However, comparisons before and after deployment showed that the artificial reefs increased local fish abundance and species richness.

noticias.titulo: Encuentran en un pueblo de Córdoba más de un kilómetro de una de las grandes carreteras del Imperio romano
noticias.resumen: Si el Imperio Romano es tu Imperio Romano, esto te interesa. No han encontrado una moneda suelta o una armadura, sino un tramo entero y localizable de una autopista de hace 2.000 años, con sus necrópolis, sus fuentes monumentales y su comercio internacional todavía escritos en el barro. En Mellaria, la actual Fuente Obejuna (Córdoba), la Universidad de Córdoba ha identificado con precisión 1.160 metros del trazado de la vía Corduba-Emerita , una de las principales arterias de Hispania. Imagina un oleoducto nacional fusionado con un corredor ferroviario de mercancías críticas, todo en la misma…
noticias.contenido: Si el Imperio Romano es tu Imperio Romano, esto te interesa. No han encontrado una moneda suelta o una armadura, sino un tramo entero y localizable de una autopista de hace 2.000 años, con sus necrópolis, sus fuentes monumentales y su comercio internacional todavía escritos en el barro. En Mellaria, la actual Fuente Obejuna (Córdoba), la Universidad de Córdoba ha identificado con precisión 1.160 metros del trazado de la vía Corduba-Emerita , una de las principales arterias de Hispania. Imagina un oleoducto nacional fusionado con un corredor ferroviario de mercancías críticas, todo en la misma calzada, y tendrás una estimación del valor. ¿Y la clave? El LiDAR , otra vez Una columna vertebral. La Corduba-Emerita unía Córdoba con Emerita Augusta, la capital de la Lusitania romana (la actual Mérida), atravesando Sierra Morena de sur a norte. Un trabajo reciente de la Unidad Patricia de la UCO y el proyecto Ager Mellariensis ha logrado identificar buena parte de sus 144 millas romanas —unos 213 kilómetros—: los investigadores la han bautizado "la autopista de los metales", porque por ella salía la riqueza minera de Sierra Morena hacia el resto del Imperio. Operación retorno . Antonio Monterroso, director de las excavaciones, la describe como "el primero de todos los viarios económicos de toda la Bética". En su apogeo, entre los siglos I y II d.C., por ella circulaban tres cargas de máximo valor imperial: cobre de Cerro Muriano y el Alto Guadiato, plata y plomo de Los Pedroches, y cinabrio y mercurio de las minas de Almadén, la antigua Sisapo, un mineral tan sensible que su transporte iba escoltado por destacamentos militares. En Motorpasión Roma construyó una carretera para llevarse la riqueza de Sierra Morena. 2.000 años después, los arqueólogos la han encontrado en Córdoba Un carro de carga pesada avanzaba entre 20 y 30 kilómetros diarios, así que recorrer los 213 kilómetros completos exigía 7-10 jornadas con relevos en postas fijas. El correo urgente imperial, cambiando de caballos, cubría hasta 150 kilómetros al día, una velocidad de comunicación que la península no volvería a igualar hasta el ferrocarril del siglo XIX. Esos minerales se reorganizaban en Corduba y bajaban por el Betis —exacto, el Guadalquivir— rumbo a Roma, hasta el punto de que, según Monterroso, sin esta vía "la capital de la Bética nunca hubiera sido tan rica". De seis a veinte kilómetros, de golpe. A través del Plan PNOA-LiDAR del Instituto Geográfico Nacional, la UCO amplió en 2024 el tramo documentado en Puente Nuevo y descubrió nuevos restos en El Bujardillo (Belmez), Los Tejares (Peñarroya-Pueblonuevo) y el Cascajoso (Hinojosa del Duque). Esto supuso un salto, de seis kilómetros conocidos a veinte , sin levantar una sola pala. Bajo Mellaria. El trazado urbano de la calzada organiza la forma de la ciudad: se conservan losas del pavimento original y hasta cuatro remodelaciones sucesivas entre los siglos III y V, superpuestas sobre capas de guijarros que forman una estratigrafía de casi dos metros de espesor. Necrópolis justa. Justo donde la vía abandonaba la ciudad por oriente, siguiendo el patrón funerario típico romano de enterrar fuera de las murallas, los arqueólogos han documentado al menos 450 metros de calzada rodeados de monumentos funerarios . Lo encontrado: un recinto de 30 por 30 metros con una edícula funeraria, fragmentos de una estatua de mármol de tamaño superior al natural y hasta cuatro "klinai" —reclinatorios donde celebraban banquetes conmemorativos en honor al difunto—, con un jardín trasero lleno de fosas rituales. Los propios excavadores lo describen como un "extravagante monumento celebrativo", excepcional no solo en Córdoba, sino en toda Hispania por su escasez. El agua, la otra obsesión romana. En 2022, en un cruce de esta misma vía dentro de Mellaria, apareció lo que Antonio Monterroso Checa calificó como el lacus (fuente pública) mejor conservado de toda Hispania : cuatro pretiles de dos metros de longitud, 1,40 metros de altura y unos 1.500 kilos cada bloque, con acueducto propio. Un año después, en 2023, se localizó también el castellum divisorium , el punto donde el agua se potabilizaba y se repartía por la ciudad mediante tuberías de plomo. Mellaria comerciaba con medio Mediterráneo. Un estudio publicado en mayo de 2026 sobre 8.839 fragmentos cerámicos recuperados en las campañas de 2022 y 2023 confirma piezas llegadas desde Italia, la Galia y el norte de África, junto a producción local de talleres béticos. Esa vía no solo transportaba meta. Es que convirtió a un pueblo cordobés en un capital nodo comercial mediterráneo. En Xataka Los mayas construyeron una ciudad perdida con pirámides de 15 metros. Y la hemos encontrado gracias a LiDAR Lo que viene ahora. El proyecto sigue activo, y con LiDAR de por medio, cada nueva campaña añade kilómetros sin apenas excavar: la ruta completa entre Córdoba y Mérida, que hace dos años era un boceto con huecos, empieza a dibujarse casi entera. Pocas veces una simple carretera cuenta tanto sobre cómo se movían las personas, el dinero y el poder en la Hispania romana.
